five_things: Lula won a fourth term in Brazil with 51.79% of the vote to Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.21%, the first Brazilian to come back from losing round one, and Bolsonaro is declining to accept the result, as family tradition dictates.
Serbia's Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat after 14 years in power as a student-led list beat his party roughly 52.7% to 39.2% in snap elections, a margin too wide to argue over.

A UN commission found that Russia's attacks on Ukraine's energy grid, including heating plants in a winter that dropped to minus 21 degrees Celsius, constitute war crimes, which the strikes have not noticeably slowed.
Anthropic filed to go public as ANT on Nasdaq, reporting $16.3 billion in first-half revenue against an $80.7 billion net loss, a ratio that makes the word 'growth' do a lot of work.
The Fed is expected to hold rates this week even though inflation has climbed to 3.7% against a 2% target, with markets betting on a hike by year-end instead.

number_of_the_day.explanation: That is Anthropic's reported net loss, which proves a company can lose more than five times its revenue and still be invited to the stock exchange.

articles.headline: Lula Wins Fourth Term After Losing Round One; Rival Asks for Do-Over
articles.dek: Brazil's 80-year-old president beat Flávio Bolsonaro 51.79% to 48.21%, a 4.4 million vote gap that his opponent says should be annulled anyway.
articles.catch_up: Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, narrowly led the first round on 4 October. Lula, who beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, then won the runoff on Sunday.
articles.why_it_matters: The result keeps Brazil, Latin America's largest economy, under a leftist government that is openly at odds with Donald Trump, while investors fret over fiscal policy. A contested loss also tests whether Brazil's institutions can withstand a second Bolsonaro refusal to concede.
body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term as Brazil's president on Sunday, taking 51.79% of the vote to Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.21%, according to The Guardian and the BBC. With every vote counted, the margin was 4.4 million. Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, declined to accept it, which in Brazilian politics is now less a reaction than a family tradition.

Lula's win is historic in two ways. He is the first Brazilian to secure a fourth term, which would run until 2030. He is also the first candidate since civilian rule returned in the 1980s to lose the first round and then win the runoff. The Guardian noted that no first-round runner-up had ever done this. Lula had trailed 47% to 45% on 4 October.

How did he do it? Mostly by persuading his own voters to leave the house. In round one, 33 million people did not vote, and abstention hit a record 21.08%. Translation: abstention means eligible voters who stay home, and The Guardian reported that this hurt Lula most because his voters tend to live farther from polling stations. In the runoff it fell to 19.21%, which the BBC described as the largest drop between rounds since 1989.

Bolsonaro's objection centers on Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin's decision to extend voting by two hours, to 7pm. He called it 'unacceptable' and said it changed the rules mid-game. Some of his supporters note that Zanin once served as Lula's lawyer. The BBC points out a complication: both campaigns had asked for an extension. Lula's team cited a lack of buses in São Paulo and Bahia, while Bolsonaro's cited heavy rain in the south and in São Paulo. Bolsonaro's speech left out that his own side had made the same request.

Observers think the challenge will fail, the BBC reported. The electoral court's president, Kássio Nunes Marques, confirmed the result and said the extension did not change the outcome. Notably, Jair Bolsonaro appointed him. A 4.4 million vote margin is also hard to blame on two extra hours of daylight.

Markets were less enthusiastic than the crowds. The BBC reported that the São Paulo stock exchange opened 15% lower, triggering a brief suspension before a slight recovery, and that interest rate futures rose as investors studied Lula's fiscal plans. Translation: traders are betting the government will spend more and that borrowing will get costlier. Lula also faces a hostile Congress, per the BBC's related coverage.

Abroad, the congratulations came from across the spectrum, including Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum, the European Commission's Ursula von der Leyen and Canada's Mark Carney. Trump, the Bolsonaro family's most important foreign ally, had not yet reacted, according to the BBC. Lula used his victory speech to say Brazil 'will not accept being anyone's backyard,' a reference to Trump's so-called 'Donroe Doctrine.'

Jair Bolsonaro, serving 27 years for a coup attempt, had hoped his son's victory would free him and perhaps give him a government role, The Guardian reported. That plan has been postponed, along with the one for the victory speech. Lula's new term starts 5 January, and the next thing to watch is whether the annulment request goes anywhere. Current odds suggest it will not.
articles.wire_headline: Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

comic.caption: Two extra hours of voting, he argues, explain 4.4 million votes. Those must have been very long hours.
comic.alt: Two bar-like stacks of ballots, one visibly taller, with a dashed gap marked 4.4M between them. A small suited official holds up a little clock labeled 2 hours and shouts that the clock did it.

articles.headline: Serbian Voters Retire Vučić, Who Had Not Planned to Be Retired
articles.dek: A student-led list took 52.7% of the vote to the ruling party's 39.2% in snap elections, and Aleksandar Vučić conceded after 14 years in power.
articles.catch_up: Protests began after a canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station and killed 16 people, an accident blamed on corruption and negligence. Aleksandar Vučić called snap parliamentary elections after roughly two years of demonstrations.
articles.why_it_matters: A government that has balanced EU candidacy against warm ties with Moscow is being replaced by one with no track record, so Serbia's course on Europe and Russia is open to change. The result is also a rare case of an entrenched leader losing a vote to a movement with no obvious leader.
body: Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić admitted defeat on Monday in snap parliamentary elections, losing to a student-led protest movement. "It is clear we have lost these elections," he said, according to the BBC. It is an unusual sentence for a man who has been in power since 2012, and he appears to have said it anyway.

The numbers were not close. With 97% of polling stations counted, the election commission said the Student List had 2.25 million votes and Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party 1.67 million. The BBC reported preliminary shares of 52.7% against 39.2%. Translation: this was not a recount situation, and there is no obvious margin to argue over.

The movement began less than two years ago after a canopy collapsed in front of the Novi Sad station and killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and negligence. Vučić and his party have repeatedly denied corruption, but voters appear to have weighed the denials against the canopy.

Vučić had served two terms as president and could not seek a third, so he led his party's list with the aim of returning as prime minister, a post he left in 2017. Translation: when the constitution limits the number of terms, the usual workaround is to move to another job in the same building. This time the voters declined to hold the door.

The Student List has no obvious leaders, and its members are not used to politics. It fielded candidates for the 250-seat parliament from across society, including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities. This is either a broad coalition or the cast of a very ambitious charity gala, and for now it is also the majority.

Its manifesto promises to purge officials who broke rules in cracking down on protesters, to stop party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and to free the public broadcaster from political control. Each pledge is a plan to remove something the previous government built. Nebojša Vladisavljević, a political scientist at the University of Belgrade, told BBC Serbian the result gave the list "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years.

The foreign reactions were revealing. Vučić backed Serbia's EU candidacy while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over the invasion of Ukraine, and both audiences are now reacting. European Commissioner Marta Kos said the door to the EU is open. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Vučić and noted that "it takes two to tango", which is the diplomatic way of saying the dance card has changed.

Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, whose party ended Viktor Orbán's 16 years in power in April, said he was delighted to hear that his victory had encouraged the students. Regional strongmen are now being retired by ballot box often enough that someone should start a support group.

Practical questions remain. The Student List must choose a prime minister, and presidential elections are due in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić filling the role in a caretaker capacity. The movement spent two years proving it could win an election. Next it has to prove it can run a ministry, which is where most protest movements find out how long the paperwork is.
articles.wire_headline: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement

articles.headline: Israel Votes After Years of War, and Gaza Wonders Whether Anyone Is Asking
articles.dek: On the eve of the general election, some Israelis want Netanyahu out, others want him kept, and Palestinians in Gaza expect little to change either way.
articles.catch_up: Israel holds a general election this week, the first since years of war that followed the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a center-right challenger who is a former general.
articles.why_it_matters: The result will shape Israel's wartime policy and its approach to Gaza, but Palestinians interviewed by Al Jazeera say a new leader would not change life under occupation. A vote that matters enormously to one population may matter much less to the one living with the consequences.
body: Israel goes to the polls this week in a general election that NPR describes, for many Israelis, as the most consequential in decades. The vote comes after years of war and the shock of the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. It is rare for a country to hold an election in which nearly everyone agrees the stakes are high and almost no one agrees on what they are.

The incumbent is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. His main challenger, according to NPR, is a center-right former general. Translation: the opposition's leading pitch is that Israel should replace a longtime political leader with a man from the military. That is not a contrast in worldview so much as a contrast in résumé, and both résumés include the word security.

Al Jazeera reported from both sides of the line on the eve of the vote. Some Israelis said they want change, with the phrase 'enough is enough' featuring in the headline. Others said they back Netanyahu to stay in power. Both groups, it seems, have reached the limit of something, and they disagree about which direction the limit is in.

In Gaza, the view is different. Al Jazeera reported that Palestinians there say a change of leadership would do little to alter the reality of life under occupation. This is a significant point about how elections work: the people most affected by a government's decisions are often not among those who get to vote for it. Gazans cannot vote in Israeli elections, so their forecast is a review rather than a ballot.

NPR's framing is that Israelis have changed after the war, and the open question is whether they will change their leadership. That is the standard test of any wartime election. Voters decide whether the people who led them through a catastrophe should be rewarded for surviving it or blamed for it, and both arguments are available to anyone with a campaign slogan.

The sources are thin on polling, coalition math and the challenger's name, so it is not possible to say here how close the race is. What can be said is that Israeli voters will choose between continuity and change, while Palestinians in Gaza have told reporters they expect the two options to look similar from where they sit. The first results will show which of those predictions needs a correction.
articles.wire_headline: ‘Enough is enough’: Palestinians and Israelis share views ahead of election

articles.headline: Machado Returns to Venezuela After Washington Apparently Finds the Right Form to Sign
articles.dek: The Nobel laureate came home to huge crowds and no arrests, while Trump said he knew nothing about it and Rubio took credit.
articles.catch_up: María Corina Machado left Venezuela in December to collect her Nobel Peace Prize, and weeks later US forces seized President Nicolás Maduro. Washington then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as interim president, leaving Machado abroad until now.
articles.why_it_matters: Venezuela's next election timeline depends on whether Washington prefers a popular opposition leader or a profitable working relationship with the current government. Oil markets and 'transition' diplomacy are both watching.
body: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado announced on Sunday that she is back in Venezuela after roughly ten months in exile. 'I'm here. With you,' she wrote on X, according to The Guardian and the BBC. She is, by the standards of this particular story, the one person who appears to have planned her own schedule.

Footage showed her at a church in Barquisimeto, in Lara state, about 220 miles west of Caracas, surrounded by supporters. The Guardian reported that the trip to the capital then took eight hours because crowds blocked streets and highways. Tens of thousands greeted her as she entered Caracas, leaning out of a car sunroof. Her ally Edmundo González confirmed the arrival and said he would soon follow.

The notable detail is what did not happen. Members of Venezuela's government had long hinted she would be arrested if she returned, but the Guardian said there was no sign of security services bothering her. Translation: when a government that threatened to detain you instead lets you pass, someone with more leverage has probably made a phone call. The BBC noted her return was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which appears to have been granted.

Washington's public position on all this is a masterclass in distributed responsibility. Asked about it, President Trump said, 'I don't know anything about it,' then added that she is 'a very nice woman' who gave him her Nobel prize, 'so how can I say anything else?' Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said her safe return was the direct result of US-supported reconciliation talks. So the White House knew nothing, and the State Department made it happen.

Some background explains the awkwardness. According to the BBC, Machado won an opposition primary in 2023 with more than 90 percent of the vote, was barred from running by Maduro's government, and her ally González ran in her place in 2024. The electoral authority declared Maduro the winner without releasing detailed tallies, while the opposition published copies of voting tallies it said showed González won. The Guardian says her movement is widely believed to have won.

After Maduro was seized in January, many expected Trump to hand power to Machado. He backed Rodríguez instead, who the Guardian says now governs what is widely seen as a US protectorate. The Guardian also reported that the administration had reportedly opposed Machado's return, fearing it would complicate its cosy relationship with Rodríguez. The BBC said reports of US involvement in delaying her return were denied by the US. Sources therefore disagree on whether Washington was an obstacle, though both agree it was relevant.

Machado has asked for fresh presidential elections by July 2027. The Guardian said it is unclear whether the administration supports that timeline, given that Trump called the oil agreement with Venezuela 'the biggest oil deal in world history.' Translation: an election might change who signs the contracts, which is a risk if the current signatories are pleasing.

Machado has praised Trump repeatedly, and in January gave him her Nobel medal, though the Nobel committee had said the prize cannot be revoked, shared or transferred. Her spokesman thanked Trump and Rubio on Sunday. Whether that gratitude is returned in the form of an election date is the thing to watch.
articles.wire_headline: Exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to rapturous reception in Venezuela

articles.headline: UN Panel Concludes That Bombing Heating Plants in Winter Is, Legally Speaking, a War Crime
articles.dek: A UN commission says Russia's attacks on Ukraine's energy grid since 2022 were war crimes, as another cold season arrives and the strikes continue.
articles.catch_up: Russia has attacked Ukraine's power and heating systems every winter since its full-scale invasion in February 2022. A UN-backed investigative body has now put its conclusions about those attacks in a formal report.
articles.why_it_matters: The finding adds a formal legal judgment to a pattern that leaves millions without heat and water in freezing weather. A report cannot restore power, but it does build a record that could matter in later prosecutions.
body: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine told the UN General Assembly on Monday that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure constitute war crimes, according to Al Jazeera. The commission said the strikes weaponise winter cold, which is a notable use of weather as a tool of policy. Translation: nature supplies the freezing, and the bombing of the heating plants supplies the rest.

The report covers attacks on heating plants, power lines and gas facilities since autumn 2022. It says the waves have grown in frequency, intensity and geographic range, with hundreds of drones and missiles launched at a time. The commission singled out the winter of 2025-2026, when temperatures fell to minus 21 degrees Celsius (minus 5.8 Fahrenheit) and millions of people faced long outages of heating, electricity, water and gas.

The legal finding is narrower than the headline suggests, and more pointed. The commission concluded that Russia committed the war crime of intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects. It assessed that the commanders ordering the strikes knew the heating facilities were indispensable to civilians. It also noted that Russian authorities had made official declarations about further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out. Translation: the commission did not have to guess at intent, because officials said some of it out loud.

Commission chair Erik Mose said that as the cold season approaches, the attacks have intensified again, raising what he called serious concerns about the threats to civilians' lives and health. The fighting shows no sign of pausing. A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia injured four people overnight, according to regional governor Mykhailo Semikin, and Moscow's defence ministry accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week.

Oleshky features in the other story of the day. NPR reported that Russia says it will open a humanitarian corridor to the occupied town, where people have been eating weeds and pickles to survive while trapped by minefields, shelling and drones. The corridor is welcome news if it opens. It is also a reminder that the party announcing humanitarian access is a party to the fighting.

The commission also accused Moscow of human trafficking in connection with recruiting foreign fighters, in violation of international human rights law. It said most of those recruited have been killed or gone missing, with others injured or captured. Al Jazeera noted numerous reports of men from India being duped into fighting on the front lines.

What happens next is mostly procedural. The commission was created by the UN Human Rights Council and can document and conclude, but it cannot arrest anyone or switch on a boiler. For now, the report is a thorough account of what the winter looks like, delivered just as the next one begins.
articles.wire_headline: Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure a war crime: UN

articles.headline: Anthropic Files to Go Public, Reports $80.7 Billion Loss Alongside $16.3 Billion in Sales
articles.dek: The Claude maker's S-1 shows revenue up from $1.2 billion to $16.3 billion in a year, a seven-founder voting bloc, and compute bills measured in hundreds of billions.
articles.catch_up: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, confidentially filed with the SEC in June, and leaked drafts circulated for weeks. On Monday it made its S-1 prospectus public, planning to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.
articles.why_it_matters: If the listing goes ahead, ordinary investors and index funds could own a piece of one of the most heavily scrutinized AI companies, but with little say over how it is run. The filing also shows how much money AI labs are committing to computing power years before they turn a steady profit.
body: Anthropic filed publicly on Monday to sell shares to the public, and it plans to trade as ANT on Nasdaq, according to TechCrunch and The Verge. The company has not said how much it wants to raise or at what price. Having already leaked most of its contents, the document arrived with the suspense of a surprise party where everyone has seen the guest list.

The headline numbers are large in both directions. Anthropic reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. It also reported a net loss of $80.7 billion. Translation: a net loss is what remains after every cost and accounting entry is counted, including ones that involve no actual cash leaving the building.

Those entries are the explanation. TechCrunch reported that the loss was largely driven by noncash adjustments tied to convertible debt, meaning loans that can turn into shares. The Verge, citing earlier Wall Street Journal reporting on the leaked drafts, said most of the loss came from accounting charges on notes the company issued to raise money. The operating loss, which tracks the actual business, was $693 million, down from $2.1 billion a year earlier. The company still says it may not achieve or sustain profitability.

The customer figures explain the revenue. As of September 30, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers paying at least $100,000 a year, more than 1,900 paying at least $1 million, and about 250 paying $10 million or more. Net revenue retention was about 900% at the end of the third quarter. Translation: existing customers, taken together, were spending roughly nine times what they had spent before, which is the sort of figure that makes a finance department either delighted or nervous, depending on which side of the invoice it sits.

TechCrunch reported that the strategy is a familiar one: get a customer in through one door, then sell them the rest of the building. More than half of customers spending $100,000 or more now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app such as Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year. The top 5% of Claude Enterprise customers using Claude Code spent about 20 times as much per month as the average enterprise user who did not use it.

The bills are on the other side of the ledger. The Verge reported commitments including about $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Anthropic also listed $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over ten years. Those three are also its distribution partners, and the filing warns they increasingly see Anthropic as a competitor and may prioritize their own needs when allocating computing capacity.

Governance is the other point of contention. Seven co-founders, including Dario and Daniela Amodei, will form a Founder LLC holding 50.1% of voting power, which Anthropic says is meant to protect its AI safety mission. A Long-Term Benefit Trust, set up in 2023, will appoint most of the board. TechCrunch noted that public shareholders will have little practical control over a company that itself acknowledges its technology poses catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

The risk factors section is candid. It mentions the possibility that AI models develop forms of sentience, AI-specific taxes, and unfavorable outcomes in copyright disputes over training data. It also says no single insurer, and potentially not the insurance industry in aggregate, could cover a catastrophic AI incident. Dario Amodei's 2025 compensation was nearly $18 million, and Daniela Amodei received $16.4 million, per the filing.

What to watch next is the price range and the size of the raise, which the filing leaves blank. Investors will then decide how much to pay for a company that has told them, in writing, about both the upside and the uninsurable downside.
articles.wire_headline: Anthropic officially files for its public debut

articles.headline: SpaceX Rents $40 Billion of Chips, Calls It Financing, Predicts Rivals Will Be Eaten
articles.dek: An Apollo-managed entity will buy the GPUs and lease them to SpaceX for about five years, while Elon Musk forecasts doom for 200-plus smaller AI landlords.
articles.catch_up: SpaceX disclosed in a regulatory filing a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and data center equipment. Apollo Global Management will buy the hardware and lease it back to SpaceX, whose AI unit includes Grok, Cursor and a cloud compute business.
articles.why_it_matters: The deal shows that cheap borrowing for AI buildouts is going to companies with large, steady revenue elsewhere, which could squeeze smaller GPU-rental firms. It also shows how much of the AI boom now runs on leases rather than cash.
body: SpaceX said Monday in a regulatory filing that it has a binding commitment for about $40 billion to pay for AI chips and related data center gear. According to TechCrunch, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management will buy the equipment and lease it to SpaceX. SpaceX called it the "largest committed GPU financing," a category that, until recently, did not need a superlative because it barely existed.

Translation: this is a very large rent-to-own arrangement for computers. Apollo, a private equity firm, pays for the chips, SpaceX uses them, and SpaceX sends back monthly checks for roughly five to five-and-a-quarter years, starting as each batch is delivered. The leases are expected to begin in the first half of 2027, and the deal is supposed to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions.

Apollo said the money will help deliver Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX's "terrestrial compute buildout." The word terrestrial is doing some quiet work there, as a reminder that this is a rocket company describing its computers by where they are not.

CFO Bret Johnsen said the lease "diversifies our funding sources" and covers a notable portion of the money SpaceX needs. He also said the company is seeing "less than one-year payback periods" on its AI infrastructure investments. Translation: SpaceX says the chips earn back their cost in under a year, which makes a five-year lease sound less like a burden and more like a generous offer from the future.

The numbers explain the appetite. TechCrunch reported that SpaceX's AI segment, covering Grok, the Cursor coding tool and cloud compute, brought in $7.6 billion of the company's $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, more than Starlink and launches combined. Capital expenditures reached nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, and Johnsen said on the Oct. 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone. A $40 billion lease, in that light, covers about one quarter of spending at the projected pace.

The timing matters because debt markets for AI infrastructure have been rough lately, as investors grow nervous about runaway spending and limited profits. SpaceX, by TechCrunch's account, had no trouble finding a lender. Its advantage is that it has other businesses, Starlink and rocket launches, producing steady cash, which lenders find comforting in the way people find a second income comforting.

Elon Musk noticed the advantage and pointed it out on X. Citing SpaceX's "investment-grade" status, he argued that debt markets have largely closed to companies lacking big revenue streams outside AI data centers. "That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation," he wrote, adding that some will survive, "but not many." Neoclouds are companies built mainly to rent out GPUs, which makes them, in structure, the same business Apollo just entered with SpaceX as its tenant.

Whether Musk is right depends on whether lenders keep treating chips as good collateral while also worrying about whether anyone will pay for what they produce. The deal itself offers one data point: at least one firm will fund $40 billion of hardware for a customer with rockets. Watch whether the neoclouds find similar landlords, or merely similar rent.
articles.wire_headline: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo

articles.headline: Meta Seeks $95 Billion From Investors, Offers Everything Except a Vote
articles.dek: The company plans to sell new shares to fund AI infrastructure, using a non-voting class that leaves Mark Zuckerberg's control untouched.
articles.catch_up: Meta is spending heavily on AI data centers and chips and now plans to raise money by selling stock, per The Information and a Meta announcement. The sales span common shares, convertible preferred shares, and a new class of non-voting stock.
articles.why_it_matters: Existing shareholders face dilution (a smaller slice of the company each), while the structure shows how founder control can survive even a giant capital raise. It also hints at how costly the AI race has become, even for one of the richest companies on earth.
body: Meta plans to sell up to $95 billion in new stock to pay for its AI buildout, according to The Information. A Meta announcement, as relayed by The Decoder, breaks the total into three pieces. It is the sort of figure that normally appears next to the word 'nation' rather than 'social network.'

The first piece is about $22.5 billion from selling Class A common stock. The second is $12.5 billion from depositary shares, each representing one-twentieth of a new preferred share. Translation: investors buy a small slice of a slightly fancier share, which Meta says will automatically turn into ordinary common stock in August 2029 unless it is converted earlier.

The remaining $60 billion is the big one. It would come from ongoing sales on the open market once new Class C shares begin trading, likely no earlier than the first quarter of 2027. Translation: Meta plans to sell shares in a steady drip, rather than all at once, which is how you raise a small country's GDP without anyone shouting.

The Class C shares are the interesting part. Meta currently has Class A shares with one vote each and Class B shares with ten votes each, and entities controlled by CEO Mark Zuckerberg hold most of the Class B. Class C, which Meta announced last week, carries no voting rights at all. That lets the company raise money without diluting Zuckerberg's control.

Put plainly, new investors are being invited to fund one of the largest infrastructure projects in corporate history in exchange for a claim on the profits and no say in how the money is spent. This is a familiar arrangement in corporate finance, and it has the pleasing property of making the word 'shareholder' mean exactly as much as the company would like it to.

There is also a circular note. According to the announcement, Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have expressed non-binding interest in buying up to $5 billion of Meta stock. These are companies that sell chips and related hardware for AI buildouts, so Meta would be raising money partly from the people it intends to pay. 'Non-binding' means they have said they are interested, not that they have signed anything.

For ordinary investors, the practical question is dilution. Issuing more shares spreads the company's earnings across a larger pile, so each existing share owns a smaller piece unless the AI spending produces enough extra profit to compensate. Meta is betting that it will. The sources do not say what happens if it does not, though the non-voting shares suggest the answer will not be decided by the people who bought them.

Watch for the first quarter of 2027, when the Class C shares may begin trading and the $60 billion drip begins. By then the market will have a clearer view of what the data centers are producing, and whether the price of admission was a bargain or merely a very large admission.
articles.wire_headline: Meta plans up to $95 billion in stock sales to fund its AI buildout

articles.headline: Microsoft Invites 60,000 Employees to Leave, Describes It as an Opportunity
articles.dek: The company is offering voluntary exits to up to 60,000 staff in four countries, months after laying off 4,800 and while its AI teams are only partly invited.
articles.catch_up: Microsoft has about 223,000 employees and has been trimming its workforce this year, including a layoff of 4,800 and a separate retirement program for long-serving staff. The new offer is a broader, voluntary version.
articles.why_it_matters: Buyouts let a company shrink headcount while avoiding the headlines of a layoff, and they show where a tech giant thinks it needs fewer people. For workers, the question is whether a voluntary offer today becomes a less voluntary one later.
body: Microsoft is offering voluntary exit packages to up to 60,000 employees in the US, UK, Canada, and India, The Verge reported. In a message to staff, chief people officer Amy Coleman described it as a chance to leave "with financial support and career planning resources." The company is, in other words, trying to reduce its workforce without calling it a layoff, which is a distinction that matters a great deal to everyone except the person leaving.

Translation: a voluntary exit offer is a buyout. The company puts a package on the table, and employees decide whether to take it. It is cheaper in public relations than a layoff, and it has the further advantage that the people who accept are the ones who already had one foot out the door. It has the disadvantage that the company does not choose who leaves.

The eligibility list is where the strategy shows. According to sources who spoke to The Verge, staff in AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance, and human resources are eligible. Cloud + AI, MicrosoftAI, and corporate, external, and legal affairs are partially participating. Marketing, the commercial business, discovery and quantum, and security are not included. So the company is encouraging departures from some of its AI teams while it spends heavily to be seen as an AI company, which is the sort of contradiction that tends to resolve itself in a spreadsheet.

The timing is not subtle. The offer arrives months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 people, mostly in Xbox and commercial sales, and Fortune reported that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is planning further layoffs. Earlier this year Microsoft also ran a voluntary retirement program for about 9,000 US employees whose age plus years of service reached 70. This one is much wider: an internal note seen by The Verge says it is not based on age, length of service, or performance.

Coleman wrote that the offer "is new for us" and that "we'll learn from it." Few employees enjoy being the pilot group for a learning exercise, but 60,000 of them now have the chance. The internal note also says Microsoft may consider another voluntary exit offer "where there is a business and workforce need," which is a polite way of saying the first offer may not be the last.

What to watch is the uptake. If too few people accept, the company still has its headcount target and several other tools for reaching it, and those tools are generally not described as opportunities.
articles.wire_headline: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees

articles.headline: OpenAI Discovers Customers Will Switch Vendors If You Pay Them to Leave
articles.dek: Discounts of up to 90 percent are pulling big accounts like Rippling, Replit and DataCamp away from Anthropic, The Information reports, at some cost to OpenAI's margins.
articles.catch_up: OpenAI and Anthropic compete to supply the AI models that power coding tools and workplace software. According to The Decoder, summarizing a report from The Information, OpenAI is now using steep discounts to win over Anthropic's largest customers.
articles.why_it_matters: A price war among AI vendors lowers costs for businesses that buy the tools, but it also shows how much of the market is being bought rather than earned. Cheap models from China add pressure on both companies.
body: OpenAI is offering discounts of up to 90 percent to lure large customers away from Anthropic, and it appears to be working, according to The Decoder, citing The Information. Rippling, Replit and DataCamp are all moving more of their AI spending to OpenAI. In the software business this is called competition. In most other businesses it is called a sale.

Rippling CEO Parker Conrad said his company raised OpenAI's share of its coding workload from 16 percent to 52 percent. Anthropic's share fell from 57 percent to 18 percent over the same stretch. Translation: the company that was doing most of the work now does about a sixth of it, and nobody had to write a farewell email.

Replit switched after OpenAI offered more than 30 percent off a contract worth over $100 million a year. That is a discount of more than $30 million, which is the sort of number that gets a procurement meeting to end early. DataCamp CEO Jonathan Cornelissen said OpenAI's pricing cut his costs by 80 to 90 percent, a figure that suggests the previous prices were less a law of nature than an opening bid.

The generosity extends to smaller buyers. A US bank with more than $7 billion in assets had its ChatGPT seats doubled to 500 employees at no extra charge, and pays under $7 per user instead of the usual $20 or more. Translation: a seat is a license for one employee to use the software, and the bank is now getting two for roughly the price of a fraction of one.

The Decoder says OpenAI is partly buying market share at the expense of its own margins. Translation: it is selling at prices that leave less profit per sale, in the hope that customers stay once they are settled in. The report also says OpenAI has achieved real price cuts through its Sol and Luna model lines, thanks to more efficient models and infrastructure, so not every discount is charity funded by investors.

Anthropic, meanwhile, saw its growth slow from the second quarter to the third, according to an investor memo cited in the report. Both companies also face pressure from China, where new models from Deepseek and Kimi reportedly deliver comparable performance for a fraction of the cost. That leaves the two American rivals fighting over customers while a third group of competitors quietly lowers what customers think the product is worth.
What to watch next is whether the customers stay when the discounts end. Loyalty in this market appears to be measured in percentage points, and at present the going rate is about 90.
articles.wire_headline: OpenAI offers discounts up to 90 percent to poach Anthropic's biggest customers

articles.headline: Tesla Cedes EV Crown, Pivots to Selling Cars That Mostly Drive Themselves, Supervised
articles.dek: With BYD now the world's largest EV maker, Tesla is betting its future on Full Self-Driving subscriptions and a possible merger with SpaceX.
articles.catch_up: Tesla lost its position as the world's largest electric vehicle maker to BYD last year, and Elon Musk has since floated a possible merger with SpaceX, days after a flying Roadster stunt. The Ars Technica report, drawing on Financial Times reporting, describes how Tesla is staking its future on autonomous driving.
articles.why_it_matters: If carmakers succeed in turning cars into software subscriptions, the vehicle you buy may become the cheaper part of what you pay for over its life. A Tesla-SpaceX merger would also concentrate more of Musk's businesses, and more of his risk, in one company.
body: Tesla, which spent years as the undisputed leader in electric vehicles, is now trying to win a different race: autonomy. According to Ars Technica, citing the Financial Times, Tesla ceded its top EV spot to BYD last year and is now leaning on Full Self-Driving software, a product whose name describes an aspiration more than a feature.

Translation: Full Self-Driving still requires a human to sit in the driver's seat and pay full attention. Tesla's supervised version costs $99 a month in the US, which makes it a subscription for the privilege of supervising.

The numbers explain the enthusiasm. Musk's earlier goal of selling 20 million vehicles a year by 2030 has been trimmed to 5 million, against 1.6 million delivered last year. Tesla said on Wednesday that it has its largest order backlog in four years, that more than 75 percent of new North American Teslas are sold with supervised FSD, and that it has 1.7 million active FSD subscriptions, up 67 percent from a year earlier. Tesla has not disclosed how much recurring revenue that produces.

Analysts see why the software matters. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives called it the "golden goose" for automakers because the margins are so high. He argued that expanding FSD from roughly 10-15 percent of customers to about 50 percent would be worth more than selling an extra 50,000 to 100,000 cars a year, because markets reward each FSD dollar 50-70 percent more than a dollar from a car sale. Translation: investors prefer money that arrives monthly and does not need a factory.

There is a catch, which is regulators. Tesla has yet to win approval for a fully autonomous version of FSD. The supervised version is approved in the Netherlands and several other European countries, but a vote of EU member states on wider rollout has been delayed until December. Xpeng, the Volkswagen-backed Chinese rival, is working with German authorities and aims for EU approval of its XNGP system after new rules are expected early next year. Its general counsel said, "We aim to be one of the first."

Cars still pay the bills for now, generating 75 percent of Tesla's revenue, and Tesla needs heavy AI spending to compete with Big Tech. That is where the SpaceX idea comes in. Musk said the companies were exploring a merger, and at the flying Roadster event he promised results from combining "the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." Supporters cite shared work on materials, AI, manufacturing and chip access. One top-15 Tesla shareholder told the FT he backed it for the AI innovations at SpaceX.

William Blair analyst Jed Dorsheimer said a deal, if approved by shareholders and regulators, could give Musk 50 percent or more of the combined company. Critics see the risk in the same place. Tesla enthusiast Max Willson warned that combining the businesses risks tying their futures to Musk's most speculative bets, and that trouble in AI could spread to otherwise strong businesses.

Rivals are watching and copying. GM hired former Tesla executive Sterling Anderson to lead product development, while BMW and Mercedes-Benz have partnered with Qualcomm and Nvidia on "Level 2 plus" systems that still require an attentive driver. Volvo's chief executive said Tesla is "probably leading the development in the West." The industry's consensus appears to be that the future is autonomous, subscription-based, and a few regulatory votes away.
Watch the EU vote in December. Until then, the car of the future remains one that drives itself while you keep your eyes on it.
articles.wire_headline: Tesla gave up the EV crown. Now it wants to win the autonomy race

articles.headline: Data Centres Unite Republicans and Democrats, Mostly Against Data Centres
articles.dek: With about 12,250 sites worldwide and 16 US states weighing bans or pauses, the buildings that run the internet have become a campaign issue.
articles.catch_up: Data centres are the warehouse-sized buildings that house the chips and servers behind the internet and AI services such as ChatGPT and Claude. They are multiplying quickly, and the BBC reports a public backlash is growing around the world.
articles.why_it_matters: The buildout shapes local electricity prices, water supplies, noise levels and job prospects, and it is now entering US midterm politics. How the fight resolves will help decide where the AI boom physically lands.
body: Data centres have become politically unpopular in the United States ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, according to the BBC. Both Republicans and Democrats are coming out against their development, which in the current climate counts as a minor miracle of bipartisanship. President Donald Trump has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", the BBC reported, which puts him at odds with a coalition that includes some of his own party.

The industry is growing quickly. Data Center Map, a company that tracks both operational and planned sites, counts about 12,250 worldwide, up from roughly 8,000 operational sites in 2021. The US leads with 4,767. Translation: the country that invented the phrase "not in my backyard" is also the one with the most backyards under construction.

The buildings are also getting larger. The biggest operational site is widely reported to be a China Telecom facility in Inner Mongolia covering about one million square metres, or roughly 140 football pitches. Larger sites are under construction, built exclusively for AI. One of them, Colossus 2, will hold hundreds of thousands of Nvidia chips and help train xAI's chatbot Grok.

That site will use 41 methane gas turbines for power. Activists say this could significantly increase local air pollution, while local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards. Both statements can be true at once, which is the usual way a standard works: it defines how much pollution counts as acceptable.

The complaints are practical ones. Data centres worldwide are thought to consume more electricity than all of France. They can use large amounts of water for cooling, which some experts say could cause shortages, and heavy demand on local grids worries people who fear higher energy bills. Neighbours also mention the noise and the amount of land the buildings occupy. Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and opposition has surfaced in Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.

Supporters respond that data centres matter for national security and AI development, and that they bring investment, tax revenue and construction jobs. A recent Brookings report, cited by the BBC, found they do create local jobs, though fewer than industry advocates claim. Hyperscale sites, run by giants such as Amazon and Microsoft, help local employment more. Colocation sites, which lease space to tenants who are not present locally, help less. Translation: a building full of computers is a poor substitute for a building full of employees.

None of this has slowed the spending. The tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn on AI infrastructure in 2026, with the total passing $1tn next year, according to the BBC. The proposed escape routes include putting data centres in space or on the Moon, where solar energy is plentiful, or shifting more AI processing onto the chips already in phones and laptops. The industry's answer to local opposition is thus to look for a location with no local residents, which is at least consistent.
articles.wire_headline: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

articles.headline: Instagram, Long Opposed to Long Videos, Discovers Long Videos
articles.dek: The platform is testing widescreen 'Features' in the US and Brazil, a format its own boss spent years arguing against.
articles.catch_up: Instagram built its business on photos and short Reels, while YouTube dominates longer video, including on living-room TVs. Instagram launched a TV app late last year and is now adding a longform format of its own.
articles.why_it_matters: If the test works, the app you open to see a friend's lunch may also want your evening, and creators will face another platform asking for longer content. For Instagram, the bet is that more watch time on TV screens matters more than keeping the feed a place for sharing.
body: Instagram announced a push into longform horizontal video, a format it calls 'Features,' according to The Verge. The test is expanding to the US in small form and is running with some creators in Brazil, spokesperson Megan Buckley told the outlet. It is a notable reversal for a company whose product has spent years teaching users that anything over a minute is a commitment.

The reversal has a personal dimension. Instagram head Adam Mosseri said in a video that he has opposed longform video on the platform 'for a long time.' His stated worry was keeping Instagram about connecting with friends and not only entertainment. Translation: people rarely send a friend a forty-minute video, and a video nobody sends is a video that generates fewer likes and shares, which are the things Instagram sells to advertisers as proof that people are enjoying themselves.

The solution, according to Mosseri, is to make shortform and longform 'symbiotic.' His examples were podcasts and comedy specials, which can exist as one long piece and also be chopped into clips. Translation: the long video is the main course, the short clips are the free samples handed out in the feed, and everyone pretends this was always the plan.

The timing makes more sense with the TV context. The Verge notes that Instagram launched a TV app late last year, starting as a Reels-focused pilot on Amazon Fire TV devices in the US. It has since expanded to Google TVs, Samsung TVs and Apple TV, and added features such as watching Stories. A vertical phone video stretched across a television is an awkward guest, and widescreen is the obvious fix.

Instagram is testing other pieces as well: clips that point viewers to a long video, a way for creators to build a 'series' of Reels, and better discovery for live video. Together they form a pipeline in which short videos lead to long ones, and long ones produce more short ones. It is a familiar loop, and YouTube has been running it for years.

Whether creators and viewers go along is unproven, since this is a small test in two countries. Mosseri's own hesitation is a reasonable benchmark. A company that spent years worrying longform would hurt friend-to-friend sharing now plans to find out by shipping it. Watch for whether the feed starts looking less like a group chat and more like a channel guide.
articles.wire_headline: Instagram chases YouTube with a push for longer, widescreen videos

articles.headline: Apple Acknowledges 'Issue' With iPhone Duo Screens, Declines to Say How Many 'Small Number' Is
articles.dek: Apple says a small number of foldables have cracked inner displays and tells owners to call AppleCare, a month into a new CEO's tenure.
articles.catch_up: Apple's iPhone Duo, a foldable phone, launched recently as one of the first major products since John Ternus succeeded Tim Cook as CEO. Users soon began posting photos of inner screens that cracked or showed a bright line after the hinge was opened.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone who paid foldable-phone prices should know that Apple is offering replacements through AppleCare, and that early reports point to a possible design flaw rather than user error. It also tests whether a new CEO's first big hardware launch can avoid an old Apple pastime: the quiet recall-shaped statement.
body: Apple has confirmed that it is aware of "an issue impacting the inner display" on a "small number of iPhone Duo units," according to statements the company gave Bloomberg and 9to5Mac, as reported by The Verge. Owners of affected phones are advised to contact AppleCare for a replacement. The statement did not say how many units are in the small number, which is how small numbers usually stay small.

The reported symptoms are specific. Users described a hinge that tightened, followed by a crack when the phone was opened, and a distinctive bright line running from the center of the display to the right side. Translation: the part of the phone that exists to fold is the part that is breaking when folded.

Apple's handling has varied by location, according to the reports. One user in Australia said an Apple Store replaced their unit "on the spot," which suggests that at least some employees have been given the authority to treat the problem as real. The Verge said it contacted Apple and had not received an on-the-record response of its own, so the company's position on the cause currently comes from statements to other outlets.

Then there is iFixit, the repair site, which published a teardown of the phone over the weekend. In cases where damage occurred, iFixit showed how the foldable screen might be pushing against a center bar. The source describes this as a possible explanation, not a confirmed diagnosis, and Apple has not said what causes the cracks. A teardown is essentially an autopsy performed by enthusiasts with small screwdrivers, and it has a way of making official statements look brief.

The timing is awkward. These are among the first devices to launch since John Ternus took over from Tim Cook, so the company's reaction will be read as an early indicator of his style. Apple's usual approach to hardware trouble is to acknowledge a narrow problem, offer a narrow fix, and avoid any word that sounds like a recall. A replacement program fits that pattern neatly.

What to watch next is whether the small number grows, whether Apple explains the cause, and whether replacement units fix the problem or simply restart the clock on it. A replaced phone with the same hinge is, after all, the same phone with a fresh opportunity.
articles.wire_headline: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens

articles.headline: RealReal Teaches Its Website to Tell Shoppers From Shopping Robots After Cart Loophole Exposed
articles.dek: After The Verge showed Meta's Muse agent could keep designer items in a cart for hours, the resale retailer tightened its bot defenses.
articles.catch_up: The RealReal, a luxury consignment retailer, puts any item in a shopper's cart on hold for 20 minutes. The Verge reported that Meta's Muse AI agent could re-add items the moment each hold expired, blocking other buyers.
articles.why_it_matters: As AI agents become mainstream shoppers, retailers must decide whether to welcome them or block them, and ordinary customers may find popular items held by software that never gets tired. Systems built on the assumption that humans are impatient are starting to break.
body: The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion retailer, said it has updated its bot defense system to make it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The move followed a Verge report showing that an agent could exploit the company's cart hold system. The retailer, in other words, has discovered that a rule written for people applies poorly to something that does not need lunch.

The mechanism is simple. According to The Verge, when an item goes into a shopper's cart on The RealReal, it goes on hold for 20 minutes, during which nobody else can buy it. Translation: the hold is a polite way of saying the handbag is yours for a moment, provided you make up your mind. Using Meta's Muse, The Verge instructed the agent to re-add listings each time the hold expired, which kept other shoppers out for hours or longer.

Chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case The Verge flagged. Its bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, he said. Agents can still surface listings and send Muse users to product pages, so the robot may browse the window but not touch the merchandise.

Friang added that the company will keep strengthening protections as AI-powered shopping evolves. Translation: this is a patch, and everyone involved expects to be patching again. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to The Verge.

The timing is awkward for everyone except Meta. The company said on its Q3 earnings call this month that shopping is the most common use case for Muse, with purchases averaging over $200, and that 10 million people in the US downloaded the app in 40 days. Tech companies are pitching agents as always-on assistants for billions of people, and it turns out that always-on is exactly the problem when a system depends on people eventually getting bored.

The larger tension is commercial. If shoppers reach websites through chatbots, retailers become one step removed from their customers, which threatens revenue such as advertising. The Verge notes that Amazon, among others, has blocked agents from shopping on its sites. Retailers must therefore choose between a new sales channel and a middleman that may quietly hoard the inventory.

The Verge observed that a person has a realistic limit on how long they will add and re-add designer clothing to a cart. An agent has no such limit. For now, The RealReal has answered with a firewall, which is the traditional response when a new customer arrives who is both very enthusiastic and not a customer.
articles.wire_headline: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing

articles.headline: Fed Expected to Hold Rates Days Before Election, Citing Purely Coincidental Calendar
articles.dek: After a September hike, the central bank is expected to pause in October as inflation hits 3.7% and oil climbs, leaving borrowers to carry the bill.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023, as inflation picked back up. Oil prices have surged because of the U.S. war with Iran, adding to price pressures.
articles.why_it_matters: A hold means credit card, mortgage and auto loan rates stay high rather than rising further, while savers keep decent yields. Anyone hoping for relief should note that no one in the sources is forecasting any.
body: The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its meeting this week, according to CNBC, even though inflation is moving the wrong way. The consumer price index rose again in September, lifting the annual rate to 3.7%, and the Fed's target is 2%. Translation: prices are rising roughly twice as fast as the central bank says it wants, and it is preparing to do nothing about it, for now.

Markets agree on the pause. Fed funds futures, which are bets on where rates are headed, priced in less than a 10% chance of another quarter-point hike this week, per the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Nearly 75% of traders expect at least one hike by year-end. That is a cheerfully specific forecast: no hike now, probably a hike soon.

The timing is awkward. The meeting lands just days before the midterm elections, and Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told CNBC that "given that it's right before an election," the Fed won't hike in October. The Fed insists it is independent of politics, which is a claim that works best when its decisions and the election calendar do not line up so neatly. CME's Mark Shore noted that the four times the Fed raised rates near a midterm, in 1978, 1982, 2018 and 2022, were all tied to rising inflation. So hiking before an election is possible, but only when things are bad enough.

Things are, arguably, getting there. Oil is the main culprit: CNBC reported that Brent crude hit a five-month high on Friday before slipping, and the latest figure we have puts it at 115.22. Higher energy costs flow into the producer price index, which measures what businesses pay, and eventually into what everyone else pays. Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave warned that if the Fed holds, markets could question its inflation-fighting credibility. Translation: if you keep promising to be tough and then wait for a better moment, traders start to notice.

For households, the mechanics matter more than the drama. The Fed's benchmark rate is what banks charge one another for overnight loans, and it feeds into credit cards, which mostly carry variable rates. A hold means card APRs stay put, at an average of 23.96% on new offers, according to LendingTree. Staying put at nearly 24% is the financial equivalent of being told the storm has stopped getting worse.

Mortgages follow a different script. They track Treasury yields, and the 10-year yield has been near 5%, which keeps the average 30-year fixed rate close to 7.4%, per Mortgage News Daily. Moody's Mark Zandi said longer-term rates have risen more than short-term ones and are weighing heavily on refinancing, homebuying and vehicle sales. In other words, the Fed can decline to hike, but the bond market will happily do some of the work for it.

Car buyers are coping by borrowing more and stretching repayment terms, according to Edmunds, a strategy that solves a monthly payment problem by making it last longer. Savers are the rare winners, since deposit yields track the Fed's rate and remain relatively attractive. Long said the outlook means "really high borrowing costs for the foreseeable future."
Watch what the Fed says about December. A pause before an election is easy to explain. A pause after it, with inflation at 3.7% and oil this high, will be harder.
articles.wire_headline: Federal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates steady in October. Here's what that means for consumers

articles.headline: Mortgage Rates Above 7% Declared 'New Normal' by Economists, Who Also Say Not to Call It That
articles.dek: Housing forecasters expect borrowing costs to stay above 7% well into 2027, ending hopes that the 3% mortgage will return from retirement.
articles.catch_up: Mortgage rates spent the years before 2022 at 3% or 4%, then jumped as inflation rose and the Fed tightened. CNBC reports that housing groups now expect rates to stay above 7% well into 2027.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone waiting for a return to pandemic-era mortgage rates may be waiting a long time, and the monthly payment on a given house will stay far higher than it was a few years ago.
body: Housing economists have settled on a phrase for mortgage rates above 7%: the new normal. According to CNBC, the term has appeared in public comments from Lawrence Yun of the National Association of Realtors and Robert Dietz of the National Association of Home Builders. Fannie Mae forecasts rates could average 7.5% in 2027, while the Mortgage Bankers Association expects them to stay above 7%. The organizations that sell and build houses, in other words, are telling buyers to get comfortable with expensive money.

The mechanism starts with the 10-year Treasury yield. Translation: the interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow for a decade, which lenders use as a yardstick for pricing mortgages. Mortgages are usually paid off or refinanced well before their 30-year term ends, so the 10-year is the closer comparison. The latest official figure puts that yield at 4.96%, which explains why a 7% mortgage does not feel like an aberration.

Inflation is the first culprit. When prices keep rising, bond investors demand higher yields to make up for the shrinking value of the money they get back later. CNBC notes that the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index, has not been below the central bank's 2% target since February 2021. Consumer price inflation was 3.74% year over year as of September, per the latest official data, so the target remains a place the economy visits only in forecasts.

The second culprit is crowding at the borrowing counter. Selma Hepp of Cotality told CNBC that heavy federal borrowing and the AI boom's appetite for data centers and power generation are competing for capital. She described a shift from a world with more capital than investment opportunities to one with tremendous competition for it. Translation: when everyone wants a loan, loans cost more, and the person buying a three-bedroom colonial is standing in line behind a server farm.

Then there is the matter of who buys mortgage bonds. Tom Graff of Facet said banks have grown wary of mortgage-backed securities after the 2022-23 rate spike produced steep losses, and the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic brought more regulatory scrutiny of bond holdings. Translation: banks got burned, and regulators are now watching them hold the matches. Meanwhile the Fed, which bought large quantities of Treasuries and mortgage bonds during the pandemic to push rates down, has stepped away from buying mortgage securities, according to TD Bank's Steve Kaminski.

Getting back to 6%, Hepp said, would likely take lower inflation, slower growth or less government borrowing pressure. Kaminski added that a weakening economy could also do it, since investors flee to Treasuries in a downturn and push yields lower. That is the housing market's current path to relief: a recession, or a miracle on the deficit.

Hepp herself objects to calling 7% the new normal, since nothing about that number is permanent. What is gone, she said, are the conditions that routinely produced 3% and 4% mortgages. For buyers, CNBC notes, waiting for much lower rates is a gamble, one in which the house is the stake and the casino is the bond market.
articles.wire_headline: Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why

articles.headline: Oil Dips 20 Cents as Saudis Visit Iran, Remains $116 Anyway
articles.dek: Brent crude slipped slightly on Monday as Saudi Arabia's defense minister held talks in Tehran, but a roughly $20 risk premium and drained inventories keep prices near records for the year.
articles.catch_up: Eight months of Middle East conflict have drained global oil inventories, and Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have recently attacked Saudi Arabia repeatedly. On Monday, Saudi Arabia's defense minister traveled to Tehran to try to cool things down.
articles.why_it_matters: Oil near $116 a barrel feeds into fuel, shipping and food costs, and with U.S. inflation at 3.74% there is little room for another supply shock. Any strike on Saudi infrastructure could push prices higher still, though CNBC's source notes prices above $120 would start destroying demand.
body: Oil prices ticked lower on Monday after Saudi Arabia's defense minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran, CNBC reported. Brent crude futures fell 20 cents to $116.52 a barrel, after briefly topping $117 earlier in the session. U.S. West Texas Intermediate dropped 79 cents to $102.48. In fairness, a 20 cent decline on a $116 barrel is the market's way of nodding politely.

The meeting also included Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, plus Pakistan's Army Chief of Staff Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence head Ibrahim Kalin. Pakistan and Turkey belong to a defense pact with Saudi Arabia. Translation: when two rivals talk, it helps to bring friends who are formally obliged to care how it turns out.

The diplomacy has a backdrop. The Houthis, who are allied with Iran, have repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. On Monday they said they fired missiles at Riyadh's international airport and launched drones at oil pumping stations. The Saudis have not confirmed that any of this happened, which leaves traders to price a rumor at $116 a barrel.

That pricing is the point. Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at Gallo Partners, told CNBC that the risk premium baked into oil is about $20 a barrel. Translation: risk premium is the extra amount buyers pay today because something worse might happen tomorrow. By that arithmetic, roughly a sixth of every barrel's price is anxiety.

The anxiety is not irrational. After eight months of conflict, global inventories have fallen sharply, and the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the government's emergency stockpile, sits at its lowest level since 1982. On Friday the Energy Department authorized releasing up to 400,000 barrels from it to address a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery. That is a small withdrawal from a shrinking account, though it does reflect the system working as designed.

Alfaro said a substantial hit to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline or more refining infrastructure could send prices sharply higher. He also said prices above $120 would destroy demand. Translation: eventually oil gets so expensive that people stop buying it, which is the market's only built-in brake and a rather painful one. He added that refining capacity is the real challenge, with problems potentially extending into 2027 and beyond.

Help from American producers looks uncertain. Alfaro said drillers are adding some rigs, but are not committing to major capital spending, or capex, amid volatile prices and geopolitical risk. Translation: oil at $102 a barrel is not enough to persuade a company to spend big, because it fears the price may not last. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia and Singapore said the kingdom will begin storing crude in Singapore from the second half of 2027, which is a long-range plan for a problem that is arriving this quarter.

Investing.com reported that UK stocks climbed as oil slipped on de-escalation hopes. Hope, it turns out, is a tradable asset, though it currently trades about 20 cents below fear. Watch whether the Houthi claims are confirmed, and whether the talks in Tehran produce anything beyond a group photo.
articles.wire_headline: Oil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate
