articles.headline: Brazil Markets Fall Sharply After Lula Wins Fourth Term, Surprising Investors Who Had Priced In Someone Else
articles.dek: Lula beat Flávio Bolsonaro 51.8% to 48.2%, the real fell 10.5%, and the Treasury cancelled two bond auctions rather than watch them happen.
articles.catch_up: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidential runoff after trailing in the first round, according to CNBC. Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly refused to concede, and Brazilian assets sold off.
articles.why_it_matters: Brazil's debt load and high interest rates mean the market's reaction affects borrowing costs for the government and for companies. Bolsonaro's refusal to concede adds political risk to an already fiscal one.
body: Brazil's Superior Electoral Court said Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the presidential runoff with 51.8% of valid votes to Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.2%, with nearly all ballots counted, CNBC reported. Lula had lost the first round three weeks earlier, and no candidate had come back from that position in a final runoff since direct elections resumed in 1989. Markets, which had apparently treated the first round as a final answer, responded with the composure of a man who has just been told the meeting was moved up.

The numbers were not subtle. CNBC reported that the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF was down 25% at 10:30 a.m. ET, and trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted by an automatic circuit breaker. Translation: a circuit breaker is a pre-agreed pause that forces everyone to stop selling and think, which in practice gives them time to think about selling more. Among U.S.-listed names, Itaú Unibanco fell 20%, Petrobras 16%, Ambev 10.3%, Embraer 5% and Vale 1.2%. The Brazilian real dropped 10.5% against the dollar to its lowest since December 2025, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC.

The Brazilian Treasury then cancelled auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate bonds scheduled for Oct. 27 and Oct. 29. Its notice said it would keep monitoring market conditions to ensure the proper functioning of the bond market. Translation: a government that sells debt would prefer not to do so on a day when buyers are holding the price they want. A separate auction of Treasury Financial Bills, scheduled for Oct. 27, is still going ahead.

The reason for the fear is fiscal. ING's Chris Turner said a 7-8% budget deficit and 70% net debt-to-GDP leave Brazil vulnerable in a global bond sell-off, and that investors would have to contend with campaign pledges such as a shorter working week without pay cuts. Citi cited concern about fiscal policy, state-owned enterprises and the reform agenda, and warned that rates staying higher for longer would hurt banks' asset quality. That explains why a bank like Itaú fell harder than a miner that sells to the world.

Analysts did not all predict disaster. The Atlantic Council's Alejo Czerwonko expects a continued gradual approach to stabilizing debt, and Goldman Sachs expects modest spending-containment measures and higher taxes, with major structural reforms unlikely. Translation: the base case is slow, imperfect budgeting, which is not a crisis but is also not what the market had paid for. Lula will also face a Congress where Bolsonaro's Liberal Party holds the largest bench in decades.

Then there is the politics. Reuters reported that Bolsonaro refused to concede overnight and said he would seek to annul the result, and called a justice's two-hour extension of voting unacceptable. CNBC noted that Lula's campaign had alleged voter suppression through suspended public transport, while Bolsonaro's campaign had also asked for more time because of rains that closed polling stations in the south. Both sides, in other words, wanted longer voting hours and only one is upset about getting them.

Markets will now watch how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the outcome, as ING's Turner put it, or allows the constitution to run its course. Leaders across Latin America largely congratulated Lula, though the result also blocks a rightward shift that Donald Trump had backed. Lula is due to govern from 2027 to 2030. The first test comes sooner: whether the Treasury can sell bonds again at a price it likes.
articles.wire_headline: Brazilian stocks rocked as Lula wins presidential election, Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede

articles.headline: Investors Discover Portfolio Without AI Performs About Same as Portfolio With AI, Which Is Awkward
articles.dek: A Goldman Sachs index that strips out AI enablers briefly beat the S&P 500 this year, as tech slides and money flees to utilities, insurers and cruise ships.
articles.catch_up: AI-related stocks have powered the S&P 500 for years, and now make up about 45% of it. This month tech has sold off, borrowing-heavy AI infrastructure firms have come under pressure, and investors have started looking elsewhere.
articles.why_it_matters: If your retirement fund is an index fund, nearly half of it is a bet on one theme, whether or not you remembered making that bet. The recent rotation shows what diversification looks like when it is suddenly needed.
body: A Goldman Sachs index that tracks the S&P 500 while excluding companies it classifies as AI enablers was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, CNBC reported. The regular S&P 500 was up 12%. The two are now roughly level after tech rallied Monday. In other words, for a brief moment, owning less of the most important technology in a generation paid slightly better than owning all of it.

The reason this is possible is concentration. Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500, according to CNBC. Translation: the index you bought to own America's 500 largest companies is closer to a very large position in a few companies that buy chips from one another. That arrangement is wonderful on the way up. This month the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7%, while other sectors have held up.

The mood has soured most in the parts of the story that run on borrowed money. CNBC reported that investors have turned against debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Meta fell almost 7% on Thursday after outlining more heavy capital spending and plans to issue additional shares. Translation: capex means spending on buildings and equipment, and issuing shares means asking investors to fund it, which they enjoy less when the bill keeps growing.

Elon Musk offered a colorful forecast on X. He said debt markets have almost entirely shut off money to any company without substantial revenue independent of AI data centers, and that more than 200 so-called neoclouds face 'guppy-level death and consolidation.' Translation: neoclouds are firms that borrow money, buy Nvidia chips, and rent out the computing power. CNBC noted that SpaceX, which Musk runs, sells computing capacity and competes with them, so the prophecy and the sales pitch happen to point the same way.

The numbers behind the worry are specific. CoreWeave and Nebius are down more than 30% over the past month and Iren is down 40%. The selloff began after the spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps reached levels generally viewed as signs of distress. Translation: a credit default swap is insurance against a company failing to repay its debt, and when the price of that insurance jumps, the people selling it are saying something.

The companies disagree with the diagnosis. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company invests in several neoclouds, told CNBC demand is 'off the charts' and that the missing piece is working capital. Nebius's Marc Boroditsky said it is not carrying CoreWeave's kind of debt. Iren's Daniel Roberts said customers are discussing multiples of all the capacity it can bring online. Note that what is missing, by Huang's own account, is money, which is the one thing a leveraged company cannot do without.

Meanwhile the money has gone somewhere duller. CNBC said State Street's consumer staples, health and utilities sector ETFs are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is up 10%, though that is tied more to the war in Iran. Oppenheimer's Ari Wald said the 'AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure,' and the firm upgraded commercial services and insurance. Berkshire Hathaway's Class B shares are up 8% this month, though they still trail the S&P 500 for the year.

Strategists are not unanimous on the sequel. MarketWatch reported that TS Lombard calls the AI theme a bubble destined to pop, but advises against trying to time it. That is useful guidance in the way that being told a storm is coming, date unknown, is useful guidance. The market data tells a mixed story: the S&P 500 proxy SPY sat at 764.9 on Oct. 26, and the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.96% on Oct. 22, which makes borrowing for data centers a more expensive hobby.

The kicker is that the safest trade of the moment includes a cruise line. Viking says much of its 2027 capacity is already booked, and Barclays upgraded it. For anyone who spent two years learning what a GPU is, the new advice is to own a boat.
articles.wire_headline: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
